scenes.name: The Yardbirds
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Salidos de la misma escena de blues del oeste de Londres que los Stones (heredaron su sitio en el Crawdaddy en 1963), dudaron entre el R&B purista y el pop; Eric Clapton se fue justo con su primer éxito y Jeff Beck abrió terreno nuevo. «Heart Full of Soul» fue de los primeros discos pop occidentales con modos indios (Beck imitó el sitar con la guitarra), «Still I’m Sad» partía de un canto gregoriano y su firma era el rave-up: blues acelerado hasta una serie de clímax, como las oleadas hormonales adolescentes. Keith Relf hablaba del pop como pintura abstracta, «imágenes en sonido». «Shapes of Things» (24 de febrero de 1966), grabado entre Chess y Columbia, es modernismo pop en su apogeo: ritmo marcial, letra filosófica y ecológica, drones de feedback y fizz casi de sitar. En la cara B, «You’re a Better Man Than I» de Mike Hugg atacaba el racismo y el militarismo.

scenes.name: Llega la psicodelia británica
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En otoño de 1966 la palabra «psychedelic» llegó a Gran Bretaña: el Melody Maker la presentó el 22 de octubre como «el gran contraataque americano» y la prensa la aplicó a los Move, Creation, los Who y los californianos Misunderstood («vamos de viaje al subconsciente»): freak-outs, volumen y asalto sonoro. Fue el momento en que empezó el rock: virtuosismo, improvisación y ambición, aún contenidos en el single. Cream, tres veteranos del R&B, sacó «I Feel Free»; Jimi Hendrix, llegado en septiembre con Chas Chandler, era el negro americano empapado de soul, blues, Dylan y ácido que los británicos imitaban: «Hey Joe» y «Stone Free» («Free Feeling»). Donovan volvió con «Sunshine Superman». El 23 de diciembre abrió UFO en el Blarney Club, la primera noche del underground, con Pink Floyd en improvisaciones de diez minutos; en Nochevieja, Psychedelicamania en el Roundhouse con los Move, Pink Floyd y los Who. Los mods quedaban atrás.

scenes.name: Blues rock británico
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: La «gramática» del heavy: su estructura de canción, sus progresiones y sus riffs vienen del blues eléctrico urbano de Muddy Waters y Howlin’ Wolf, pero de segunda mano, ya «rockeado» por los grupos británicos de guitarra. El gran mediador son los Yardbirds y su sucesión de solistas (Eric Clapton, Jeff Beck y Jimmy Page), que veneraban a los bluesmen negros sin imitarlos servilmente. Cream (y Clapton, según él mismo) inventa el solo largo para estirar media hora de repertorio, y el público lo convierte en convención. El virtuosismo de la guitarra solista es la mayor herencia del blues rock al heavy.

podcast.title: Critic of Eddie Van Halen's "Feeling"
podcast.body: Clapton remarked that Eddie Van Halen was "technically good but lacks feeling." One historian interpreted this as Clapton asserting his own greater "authenticity to the blues." However, this perspective is challenged by the observation that Clapton, a white man who built his career on blues music, might be better described as "blues inspired" rather than an "authentic blues guitarist," given the derivative nature of rock music. "But Clapton has said that he thinks Eddie Van Halen is technically good but lacks feeling which one historian has interpreted as Clapton thinking that he himself is more authentic to the blues."

podcast.title: Early Adopter of Wah-Wah Pedal
podcast.body: Eric Clapton, described as a "hot new player from the UK," was one of the two influential guitarists Henry Goldrich convinced to purchase a wah-wah pedal at Manie's Music in the mid-1960s. His adoption of the pedal was instrumental in shaping his playing and the broader sound of guitar-based rock and roll. "One was up and coming guitarist named Jimmy Hendrix. And then there was Eric Clapton, a hot new player from the UK. They each bought, okay, this thing sounds cool. Give me one."

xref.title: Jim Gordon Death (March 13, 2023) – Died of Natural Causes in Psychiatric Prison at 77; Killed Mother in 1983
xref.body: Jim Gordon was a highly respected session drummer in the 1960s who played on dozens of recordings and performed with Eric Clapton in Derek and the Dominoes, including on the classic "Layla." He then developed severe schizophrenia — voices told him to starve himself, he couldn't sleep, was alcoholic, and received the wrong treatment. On June 3, 1983, a voice told him to attack his mother with a hammer and stab her to death with a butcher knife. He did. He was sentenced to prison and denied parole at least 10 times due to the severity of his mental illness; he remained in a psychiatric facility until he died of natural causes on March 13, 2023, at age 77. "A voice told him to attack his mother with a hammer and stab her to death with a butcher knife. So he did."

xref.title: Falsified Live Recording of "I Am the Walrus"
xref.body: The alleged live recording of "I Am the Walrus" released on the 1994 *Cigarettes & Alcohol* EP was later exposed as a fabrication. It was not recorded live at the Cat House in Glasgow in June 1994 as claimed, but rather during a drunken sound check for a Sony convention at the Glen Eagles Hotel in 1993. The band intentionally misrepresented its origin to enhance their image, even incorporating crowd noise taken from a 1973 Eric Clapton/Faces bootleg.

xref.title: Pioneer of Wah-Wah Pedal on Record
xref.body: Jimi Hendrix was one of the first, if not *the* first, artists to incorporate the wah-wah pedal into his sound, particularly on record. While Eric Clapton also used it around the same time on "Tales of Brave Ulysses," Hendrix's "Burning the Midnight Lamp" (a B-side) was released within days of Clapton's track in the spring of 1967, marking a pivotal moment in guitar effects. "Jimmy was right there when the wall-watt pedal came in in 1967."

xref.title: Profound Influence on Blues and Rock Pioneers
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe had a deep impact on the trajectory of the blues and on the pioneers of rock and roll, including major figures like Little Richard, Chuck Berry, Jerry Lee Lewis, and Johnny Cash, all of whom were ardent fans. Her work also captivated British musicians such as Keith Richards, Eric Clapton, and Jeff Beck. "What is not in dispute is that sister Rosetta Tharp had a profound effect on the course of the blues, and then with the pioneers of rock."
